narrative:
Short impact summary

Advances in Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining has achieved clear scholarly uptake since its 2020 publication, with 23 OpenAlex citations and a field-year percentile that places it in the top 10% of works in its cohort. The record also suggests broad topical reach across data mining, knowledge extraction, information retrieval, and data science.

Full narrative

Published by Springer Nature in the Lecture Notes in Computer Science series, this scholarly book has developed a measurable citation footprint that signals active use in subsequent research. The citation trajectory is strongest in recent years, with most citing works appearing in 2022–2024, indicating that the book’s relevance has persisted and, in the available record, grown over time.

The citing landscape shows that the book is being drawn into a wide range of technical work rather than a single narrow niche. Recent citations appear in articles on relation extraction, machine learning for battery state estimation, multimodal fusion, graph neural network-based recommendation, EEG-based emotion recognition, sparse representation, causal inference for recommendation, and financial risk assessment. This pattern points to the book’s utility as a reference point for methods and problems across contemporary computer science and data-driven research.

Geographically, the citing literature is concentrated in China, with additional citations distributed across Canada, France, Ghana, Zambia, Australia, Germany, Spain, and other countries. Most citing works are journal articles, with a smaller number of conference papers and preprints, and they appear in venues including Information Processing & Management, Applied Sciences, Neural Networks, and Expert Systems with Applications. Taken together, this suggests adoption across mainstream scholarly channels in the field.

Other signals in the record are more limited but still informative. OpenAIRE identifies the work as a closed book and conference object record, and WorldCat holdings indicate library discoverability. No event data is available, so the public-facing discussion record is thin in this digest; the strongest evidence of influence is therefore scholarly citation and disciplinary reuse rather than recorded events or broader media attention.
